newsitem.title: USA: FCC proposes captioning for most TV shows.
newsitem.headline: FCC proposes captioning for most TV shows.

text.p: Regulators Thursday proposed helping people with hearing disabilities by requiring television stations and cable TV operators to provide closed captioning for most programs within eight years.

The majority of shows on the big broadcast networks already are closed captioned, according to the Federal Communication Commission. The FCC proposal would be felt mostly by programmers who provide shows to cable and satellite TV networks.
The plan, which would implement a provision of last year's communications bill, would exempt programs that face an "undue financial burden" from the rules.
The exemption could be based on a show's audience rating or the relative size of a TV station or cable operator's viewing market, among other factors.
Smaller markets, for example, earn smaller revenues and could therefore be exempted. Foreign-language programs that serve a small audience also could be exempt.

Closed captioning, which can cost up to $2,500 an hour for some shows, resembles subtitles and helps viewers by identifying spoken works. It also can identify the person who is speaking, sound effects, music and laughter.
A viewer wishing to see the closed captioning must use a set-top decoder or a television with a built-in decoder.
An estimated 50 million to 60 million homes currently can receive closed captioning.
Nearly 30 percent of the prime-time programming on the top 20 basic cable networks and more than 60 percent on the top six premium networks are closed capitioned, the FCC said.
The FCC proposed that TV stations and cable operators "ultimately" be responsible for complying with the rules. But producers of the programs would be responsible for captioning them.
All new programs that are not exempt from the rules would be closed captioned within eight years. The FCC also is studying a 10-year transition.
Under the eight-year plan, the FCC proposed to phase in the rules by increasing the amount of required captioning by 25 percent every two years.
The agency also sought comment on whether exemptions should be based on market size, a program's audience rating or share, or other factors. A number of factors could be used.
The FCC said that for a previously taped show, such as a situation comedy, it can cost anywhere from $800 to $2,500 an hour to provide closed captioning.
The cost for a "live" show, such as a sporting event or a talk show, ranges from $120 to $1,200 an hour.

National Cable Television Association President Decker Anstrom said, "We look forward to reviewing the (proposal), and we're committed to help the commission craft rules that result in more closed captioning on television."
But he added that his group also "will encourage the FCC to continue to recognize the challenges that face the diverse cable programming industry."
